content: Ascariasis is a helminthic infection that occurs globally and is the most common parasitic worm infection in humans. The infection is transmitted primarily through the hand-to-mouth route, and humans are the only known host for the parasite. Ascariasis is more prevalent in tropical regions and predominantly affects children. The scientific study of Ascaris lumbricoides, the nematode responsible for ascariasis, was advanced by Edward Tyson, and the disease has been recognized for many years. The infection begins when a person ingests eggs of the parasite, typically through contaminated food or water. Once ingested, the eggs hatch into larvae in the intestine. These larvae penetrate the intestinal mucosa and are carried via the portal and systemic circulation to the lungs. In the lungs, the larvae mature further, penetrate the alveolar walls, and ascend the bronchial tree to the throat, where they are swallowed. Upon returning to the small intestine, the larvae develop into adult worms, which can live for 1 to 2 years. Ascariasis is caused by the soil-transmitted helminth Ascaris lumbricoides. It can mimic other parasitic infections or gastrointestinal conditions such as peptic ulcer disease, intussusception in children, or bile duct stones. The disease affects at least 1 billion people worldwide, with approximately 4 million cases in the United States. It is most common in children aged 2 to 10 years and is three times more prevalent in African-Americans compared to Caucasians. Risk factors include poor sanitation and environmental contamination with feces. Most cases of ascariasis are asymptomatic, with over 80% of infected individuals experiencing minimal or no symptoms. However, complications can occur when adult worms migrate to organs such as the bile duct, pancreas, or appendix. A high worm burden can lead to intestinal obstruction. While the prognosis is generally good, severe cases can result in mortality, with up to 60,000 deaths annually. Approximately 6% of hospitalized patients with complications die from the infection. Symptoms, when present, may include mild pulmonary and abdominal complaints such as cough, dyspepsia, and nausea. Severe cases can involve mechanical obstruction of a viscus, leading to significant clinical manifestations. Physical examination findings vary depending on the worm burden and the organs involved. Abdominal tenderness may occur due to complications such as intestinal obstruction, appendicitis, biliary colic, acute cholangitis, acute cholecystitis, or hepatic abscess. Diagnosis is often made through microscopic identification of eggs in the feces. Chest X-rays may show oval or round infiltrates of varying sizes, indicative of Löffler's syndrome, which typically resolves spontaneously. Abdominal radiographs and contrast studies can reveal worm masses in bowel loops. CT scans with contrast can identify worms in the gastrointestinal tract, while ultrasonography can detect worms in the biliary tree, pancreatic duct, and bowel loops. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) can also identify worms in the pancreatobiliary tract. All cases of ascariasis, whether symptomatic or asymptomatic, should be treated with antimicrobial therapy. Albendazole is the treatment of choice, although other anthelmintic medications are also effective. Due to the high rate of reinfection, repeat treatment may sometimes be necessary. While medical therapy is the primary management approach, surgery may be required in cases where medical treatment fails or complications arise. Indications for surgical intervention include complete intestinal obstruction with inadequate decompression, volvulus, intussusception, intestinal perforation, acute appendicitis, or worms trapped in ducts. Prevention of ascariasis is best achieved through improvements in personal hygiene and environmental sanitation.
